name: Tzotzil, Zinacantán
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz; además hay un acento aun más fuerte que acompaña la última sílaba de una frase o una oración (puede consistir en una sola palabra, pronunciada aisladamente, o en palabras enunciadas con el mismo aliento). [...] Aquí el símbolo / representa el acento de la palabra, y el símbolo // representa el acento de la frase, que es todavía más enfático. Es claro que las partículas no se acentúan salvo que estén en la posición final.
new_statements.translation: The primary accent of a Tzotzil word falls on the first syllable of the root; in addition there is an even stronger accent that accompanies the last syllable of a phrase or sentence (which may consist of a single word, pronounced in isolation, or of words uttered in the same breath). [...] Here the symbol / represents the accent of the word, and the symbol // represents the accent of the phrase, which is still more emphatic. Clearly the particles are not accented unless they are in final position.
new_statements.citation: Haviland, John B. 1981. Sk'op Sotz'leb: El Tzotzil de San Lorenzo Zinacantán. México: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Filológicas, Centro de Estudios Mayas. Cap. I, Notas sobre la fonología, p. 14.
new_statements.locator: Capítulo I (Pronunciación), p. 14, paragraph beginning 'El acento primario' and the paragraph after the five examples
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (9-page scan, no text; Acrobat scan 2003) and read PDF page 7 = printed pp. 14-15 on the saved page scan. Running head 'EL TZOTZIL DE SAN LORENZO ZINACANTAN', page number 14. The quoted passage is there word for word: paragraph 'El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera silaba de la raiz; ademas hay un acento aun mas fuerte que acompana la ultima silaba de una frase o una oracion (puede consistir en una sola palabra, pronunciada aisladamente, o en palabras enunciadas con el mismo aliento). Por ejemplo, veanse las frases siguientes:', then the five examples with / and // marks (jvabajom, li jvabajome, Chtal li jvabajome, Chtal xa li jvabajom 'une, 'Ali jvabajome, cht…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level primary stress sits on the first syllable of the lexical root, so inflectional/possessive prefixes (j-, s-, ch-, i-, ta x- etc.) are skipped: jvábajom 'musician' (root vab/vob), chtál 'he comes' (root tal-). A separate, stronger phrase accent falls on the last syllable of the intonational phrase/sentence, so a word said in isolation carries final prominence (jvábajóm; li jvábajomé). Laughlin 1975:23 states the same two-level system from the other end: final-syllable stress on words in isolation, but in running speech stress on the root vowel (the first if the root has two) and at phrase end.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary word stress described. Haviland distinguishes two degrees: word accent (/) on the root-initial syllable and a stronger phrase accent (//) on the phrase-final syllable; a word can carry both (jvábajóm). Particles are unaccented except in phrase-final position (Chtál xa li jvábajom ʔuné).
new_statements.exceptions: Haviland: particles are unaccented unless phrase-final. Laughlin 1975:23: in isolation forms, stress is not final in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated two-syllable stems (marked with an acute accent in the dictionary).
new_statements.domain_note: Two domains are explicitly separated: word (root-initial accent) vs phrase/sentence (final-syllable accent, the stronger of the two). Citation forms in isolation therefore surface with final prominence (Laughlin: 'primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation'), which is the phrase accent, not the word accent; a catalog entry based on citation forms would read fixed: final syllable, one based on the word-level rule reads root-initial (morphologically determined, since prefix syllables such as ch-i-, ta x-, li are skipped rather than counted). Aissen 2017:241 gives the same two-level summary and notes stress is predictable and unmarked in the orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand sources describe exactly this lect: Haviland 1981 is titled 'El Tzotzil de San Lorenzo Zinacantán' and Laughlin 1975 'The Great Tzotzil Dictionary of San Lorenzo Zinacantán'. Glottolog files it as a bookkeeping dialect of Tzotzil (tzot1259); the StressTyp2 entry for this language 'Tzotzil, Zinacanteco' carries the English wording of the same Haviland statement (from the on-line English edition of the grammar). Statements for other dialects (Cowan 1969 Huixtán; Delgaty & Sánchez 1978 San Andrés; Herrera Zendejas 2014/2019 Venustiano Carranza = 'San Bartolo') are not used here.

new_statements.quote: The primary accent of a word in Tzotzil falls on the first syllable of the root; there is also an even stronger accent that accompanies the last syllable of a phrase or sentence (it can consists of a single word, pronounced in isolation, or of words uttered in the same breath). For example, see the following phrases [...]: jvabajom 'musician'; li jvabajome 'the musician'; Chtal li jvabajome. 'The musician is coming.'; Chtal xa li jvabajom `une. 'Well, the musician is coming'; `Ali jvabajome, chtal xa. 'The musician, he's coming already.' Here the symbol / represent word, and the symbol // represents phrasal accent, which is even more emphatic. It is clear that particles are not accented unless they are in final position.
new_statements.citation: Haviland, John B., Stuart Robinson & Esteban Gutierrez. n.d. An On-line Tzotzil Grammar (Sk'op Sotz'leb, English edition of Haviland 1981), Chapter 1 'Notes on Phonology', section 1.2 'Stress and Intonation'.
new_statements.locator: Chapter One 'Notes on Phonology', section 1.2 'Stress and Intonation' (unpaginated web page; archived copy (Internet Archive, 30 Jun 2017) ofhttp://zapata.org/tzotzil/Chapters/chapt1.html); the HTML transcription has lost the accent marks that the printed Spanish edition (p. 14) puts on the examples

For example, see the following phrases (which can be heard as a.WAV file):' then a two-column table (jvabajom / musician; li jvabajome / the musician; Chtal li jvabajome. / The musician is coming; Chtal xa li jvabajom `une. / Well, the musician is coming; `Ali jvabajome, chtal xa.…
new_statements.relation_note: Verbatim English rendering of the existing statement (Haviland 1981, Cap. I p. 14, Spanish): word accent on the first syllable of the root, plus a stronger phrase-final accent; particles unaccented unless phrase-final. Same placement and same two-level (word vs. phrase) description; adds nothing beyond the translation. The on-disk Spanish original matches sentence for sentence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (so prefixes are skipped: s-NA, ch-TAL, j-VAbajom); on top of that, the last syllable of a phrase or sentence — including a word spoken in isolation — carries a stronger phrasal accent. Grammatical particles carry no accent unless they end the phrase.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; the only second prominence is the phrase-final accent (marked //), which is stronger than word stress (marked /).
new_statements.exceptions: Particles are not accented unless they are in phrase-final position; no lexical exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: The Haviland grammar (both the 1981 Spanish original and the on-line English edition) explicitly describes 'The Tzotzil spoken in Zinacantan (that is, Zinacantec Tzotzil)' — the tzot1264 variety. The item behind work 0's URL, Polian 2024, describes the Venustiano Carranza ('tseltal'-called) southern Tsotsil variety, a different lect from Zinacantán; it was not read. Cowan 1969 (SIL) is a general Tzotzil grammar whose dialect base could not be checked because the file is inaccessible.

sources.citation: Aissen, Judith. 2017. Special clitics and the right periphery in Tsotsil. In Claire Bowern, Laurence Horn & Raffaella Zanuttini (eds.), On looking into words (and beyond), 235-262. Berlin: Language Science Press. p. 241.
sources.note: p. 241: 'Descriptions of Z Tsotsil characterize prosodic prominence at two levels – the word and the phrase. At the word level, stress falls on the initial syllable of the root; at the phrase level, it falls on the final syllable of the ιP (Laughlin 1975,23; Haviland 1981,14) (stress being predictable, it is not marked in the orthography).' Fn. 7: same phrase-final prominence reported for other Tsotsil dialects (Cowan 1969: 4; Delgaty & Sánchez 1978: 11). Second-hand but by a specialist on this lect; agrees with both primaries.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514. §6.1 Stress, pp. 495-496.
sources.note: Family survey: cites Haviland 1981 among Greater Tseltalan descriptions of phrase-medial initial/root stress vs phrase-final stress ('Similar patterns have been noted for Greater Tseltalan languages (.. Haviland 1981..)'); notes phonetic correlates of Mayan stress are underdocumented and that Herrera Zendejas 2014 gives limited instrumental data on Tsotsil (Venustiano Carranza dialect, not Zinacantán). No Zinacantán-specific statement.

sources.citation: Laughlin, Robert M. 1975. The Great Tzotzil Dictionary of San Lorenzo Zinacantán (Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 19). Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press. Explanatory Notes, p. 23.
sources.note: p. 23 (verified on page scan): 'Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables. In the latter instances, the stress is indicated by an acute accent. In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase.'
